analysis.one_liner: Caps compensation for pain and suffering in malpractice lawsuits over obstetric and gynecological care at $250,000.
analysis.headline: The Senate blocked the bill from ever reaching the floor, failing a procedural vote 48-45 when 60 votes were needed; it died without a debate or an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits over negligent obstetric and gynecological care nationwide. It kept full payment for measurable losses like medical bills and lost wages, but capped 'pain and suffering' compensation at $250,000, tightened deadlines for filing suit, restricted what injury victims' lawyers could be paid, cut awards by the amount of any insurance benefits a victim had already received, and barred punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved OB/GYN drugs and devices. It would have overridden state laws that offered stronger protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurers who sell medical malpractice policies, obstetricians and gynecologists facing premiums, and makers of obstetric and gynecological drugs and devices. All three would gain because the amounts they pay out after an injury would shrink and their court exposure would narrow.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Malpractice insurers, OB/GYN physicians, drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Keeps unlimited recovery of economic damages — medical bills, lost earnings, and care costs — so patients' measurable losses stay fully compensable.
Caps noneconomic damages at $250,000 on the theory that lower liability costs would ease the burden the bill says the system places on the delivery of obstetric and gynecological services.
Limits plaintiffs' attorneys' contingency fees on a sliding scale, so more of any award reaches the injured patient rather than the lawyer.
Requires future damage awards of $50,000 or more to be paid in periodic installments at any party's request, giving defendants with adequate insurance or assets more time to pay.

analysis.who_pays: Women and infants injured by negligent obstetric or gynecological care. Their compensation for pain, disfigurement, mental anguish, and loss of enjoyment of life would be capped at $250,000 regardless of how severe the harm, their awards would be reduced by any insurance or public benefits already received, and they would face shorter filing deadlines and stricter expert-witness rules. State laws giving stronger protections would be preempted.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured during childbirth and gynecological care

drawbacks.text: Birth-injury and gynecological negligence cases often turn on exactly the damages this bill caps: a $250,000 ceiling on pain and suffering applies no matter how severe the injury, and the jury is not even told the limit exists.

Awards must be reduced by any collateral source benefits the claimant is entitled to, such as health insurance or workers' compensation payments, even though the claimant or their family paid premiums to obtain those benefits.

Punitive damages are essentially barred against manufacturers of OB/GYN products that comply with FDA standards, removing the strongest financial deterrent against defective drugs and devices, with exceptions only for fraud on the FDA or bribery.

The rules preempt state law, overriding any state that offers stronger protections to patients, while expressly preserving any state law that gives providers or manufacturers greater protection from liability than the bill itself.

Supporters' premise — that liability costs were choking off obstetric care — was disputed at the time; the bill's floor debate turned on whether insurance-market problems rather than jury awards were driving premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to patients are real but narrow: economic losses stay fully compensable, fee limits put more of any award in the patient's pocket, and supporters argued lower premiums would keep obstetricians in practice. But the costs fall on the people the bill is nominally about — the woman or infant harmed by negligent care — who would absorb the capped pain-and-suffering award, reduced awards, and a shield for FDA-approved products. On balance the bill traded patient compensation for relief to insurers, physicians, and manufacturers, and its own text preserved state protections for providers and manufacturers while overriding protections for patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a real debate: a motion just to begin considering it failed a procedural vote that needed 60 senators, getting only 48, and the motion was then withdrawn.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the bill in the Senate on February 10, 2004, and it was placed on the Senate calendar within two days.
On February 12, 2004, a motion to proceed to consideration was made and a cloture motion — the procedure that requires 60 senators to cut off delay — was filed on it.
The Senate debated the motion to proceed over two days, February 23 and 24, 2004.
On February 24, 2004, the cloture motion failed 48-45: 47 of 51 Republicans voted yes but only 1 of 48 Democrats joined them, leaving the bill short of the 60 votes needed to begin consideration.
The motion to proceed was withdrawn the same day, and the bill received no further action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured during childbirth and gynecological care keep today's compensation rules in their states, because the bill died before any chamber voted on it. The insurers, physicians, and manufacturers who would have paid less after injuries gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients; insurers and providers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed the motion to proceed to bring it to the floor.

for.name: 13 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all 13 of them Republicans.

for.name: 47 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on cloture to begin considering the bill.

for.name: American Medical Association and physician groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for federal malpractice damage caps, citing rising liability premiums and ob-gyns leaving practice.

against.name: 41 of 48 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the cloture motion, denying the bill the 60 votes needed to begin consideration.

against.name: 3 of 51 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cloture, joining Democrats in keeping the bill off the floor.

against.name: Sen. James Jeffords
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the cloture motion.

against.name: Trial lawyers and patient-advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal damage caps and preemption of state malpractice law, arguing they strip compensation from catastrophically injured patients.

sides.party_line_note: The 48-45 vote split almost entirely by party: 47 of 51 Republicans voted yes and 47 of 48 Democrats plus the one Independent voted no, with one Democrat and three Republicans crossing lines.

industries.note: Damage caps, collateral-source offsets, and stricter procedures directly reduce what insurers pay on obstetric and gynecological claims. Their gain comes out of compensation that injured patients would otherwise receive.

The bill would cap the pain-and-suffering awards that drive malpractice premiums, on the theory that relief would keep ob-gyns in practice. The relief is funded by reducing what negligent-care victims collect.

industries.industry: Drug and device makers of OB/GYN products
industries.note: Manufacturers of FDA-approved products would be immune from punitive damages, and prescribing providers could not even be named in product-liability suits, sharply cutting their litigation exposure.

Mandatory sliding-scale contingency fees and a $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages would cut the fees recoverable in exactly the cases trial lawyers handle. Their interest in opposing the bill ran alongside injured patients' interest in full compensation.
